title: Area V review: Navigation Systems
intro: These questions mix both Tasks of Area V, from VOR, DME and GPS navigation to departures, airways and arrivals. Many of them put the two Tasks together in one IFR flight situation, just like the checkride.

questions.q: You filed a direct route from one VOR to another, off airways. Center has just said "radar service terminated." Nearing the second VOR, the needle starts to swing. What is required, and when are you over the station?
options: No report on a direct route. You are over it when the NAV flag drops into view.
No report, since it is not a solid triangle. You are over it when the needle swings.
Report over the VOR. You are over it as soon as the needle first starts to swing.
Report over the VOR, since it defines your route. You are over it when TO/FROM reverses.
questions.why: On a direct route you must report over each point used to define the route [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2c2]]; those fixes become compulsory reporting points unless ATC says otherwise [[29:81|IPH 2-21]]. Reports resume after "radar service terminated" [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2c3]]. Needle swings can be brief roughness, so use the TO/FROM indicator for positive station passage [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3e2]]. Report the time of the first complete TO/FROM reversal [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2a1]].

questions.q: ATC clears you to join the 160° radial inbound to a VOR (course 340°). You center the needle with FROM and find you are on the 100° radial. Using the IFH method, what heading do you fly to intercept?
questions.why: The difference is 160 - 100 = 60°. Doubled, that is 120°, but the intercept angle is never more than 90° [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Facing inbound, the 160° radial is to your left, so turn 90° left of the 340° course: 340 - 90 = 250°. 220° uses the 120° angle, 280° just flies at the station, and 070° points the wrong way.

questions.q: Takeoff minimums for your runway read "Standard with minimum climb of 400' per NM to 3000." The ODP is part of your clearance. You expect a 120 knot groundspeed in the climb, and today the POH shows about 650 fpm. What is true?
options: You need about 480 fpm at 120 knots, so 650 fpm is plenty.
You need 800 fpm, but only until you are turning on course.
Part 91 pilots may ignore the climb gradient, so you may depart.
You need 800 fpm and can't make it, so wait until you can.
questions.why: Convert the gradient: 400 ft/NM x 120 knots / 60 = 800 fpm, the same thing the TPP rate of climb table does [[29:34|IPH 1-18]]. A published climb gradient is mandatory when the procedure is part of your ATC clearance [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e5]]. If you can't meet the ODP gradient, wait until you can depart in VMC [[29:59|IPH 1-43]].

questions.q: You tune a VORTAC to identify an en route fix by its radial and DME. You hear only the higher-pitched ident, about once every 30 seconds. What does this tell you?
options: Both parts work. That is the normal ident pattern for a VORTAC.
The DME is out. Use the radial for the fix, not the distance.
The DME works, but the VOR does not. Don't use the radial.
The station is in test mode, but both parts are still usable.
questions.why: The DME ident is the higher tone, heard once for every three or four VOR idents. If you hear only one ident about every 30 seconds, the DME works but the VOR does not [[23:260|IFH 9-17]]. Without the radial you have only a distance, and one NAVAID alone can't pin down the fix [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

questions.q: Climbing via an RNAV SID, departure says "Turn left heading 240, climb and maintain 7,000." The controller does not say "expect to resume SID." The next SID fix has an "at or below 5,000" restriction. What do you do?
options: Fly heading 240, but level at 5,000 until you pass abeam the next fix, then climb.
Fly heading 240 and climb to 7,000. The SID and its restrictions are canceled.
Stay on the SID path to the next fix at 5,000, then turn to heading 240 and climb.
Fly heading 240 and climb to 7,000, but keep the published SID speed limits.
questions.why: Once you are vectored off a SID, consider it canceled unless ATC adds "expect to resume SID." Its published altitude and speed restrictions are canceled too, and ATC gives you an altitude and, if needed, a speed [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h3]].

questions.q: You fly the airway in this picture. At the changeover point you tune the VOR ahead. The needle centers nicely, but the ident is T-E-S-T. You also have an IFR GPS that is a suitable RNAV system. What is your best plan?
options: Use the VOR ahead, since the needle centers and the signal is strong.
Keep using the VOR behind you all the way to the next station.
Don't use the VOR ahead. Use the GPS as a substitute and tell ATC.
Descend to the MOCA to get a stronger signal from the VOR ahead.
questions.why: A T-E-S-T code means the facility is off the air for maintenance and may be unreliable even if you receive a signal [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]. A suitable RNAV system may substitute for an out-of-service VOR, and you may need to advise ATC [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3a1]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3a Note 3]]. The COP exists so you don't lose guidance at the MEA, so staying on the station behind is not the answer [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6]].

questions.q: You are flying a 10 DME arc in non-radar airspace. The DME groundspeed reads 35 knots. You filed a true airspeed of 120 knots, and your TAS is still 120. Must you report a speed change to ATC?
options: No. The report is for TAS; DME groundspeed means little on an arc.
Yes, but only once you are back in radar contact and on the airway.
Yes. Your groundspeed is more than 10 knots below the flight plan TAS.
No. Speed changes are reported only to Flight Service, not to Center.
questions.why: You report when your average true airspeed at cruise changes by 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater, from the flight plan [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(e)]]. Your TAS has not changed. DME groundspeed is accurate only when you fly directly to or from the station, so on an arc it means little [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].

questions.q: You fly IFR off airways in uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 ft. Your magnetic course is 175°. A strong west wind makes your heading 188°. Which cruising altitude fits the rule?
questions.why: In uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 ft MSL, a magnetic course of 0° to 179° calls for an odd thousand foot altitude [[60:481|14 CFR 91.179(b)(1)]]. The rule uses magnetic course, not heading, so 175° means odd thousands: 5,000 ft. Half-thousands are VFR altitudes, not IFR. In controlled airspace you would fly the altitude ATC assigns [[60:480|14 CFR 91.179(a)]].

questions.q: Your 30-day VOR check is due. At the departure airport you taxi to the designated surface checkpoint, which lists the 150° radial. With the CDI centered and FROM showing, the OBS reads 155°. What now?
options: Legal. Every type of VOR check allows up to 6°, so just log it and go.
Not within limits. Get the receiver fixed before VOR IFR flight.
Legal, but only if a second VOR receiver agrees with it within 4°.
Legal if you set the OBS 5° off from now on to correct for the error.
questions.why: A surface checkpoint allows ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(2)]]. Only a designated airborne checkpoint allows ±6° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]]. With more than ±4° on a ground check, don't fly IFR until the source of the error is fixed, and don't apply your own corrections beyond the manufacturer's correction card [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].

questions.q: You fly a T-route far from any airport. Your GPS CDI is at en route sensitivity, and the needle sits at three-quarter scale. About how far off the centerline are you?
options: About 3.75 NM
About 0.75 NM
About 7.5 NM
About 0.23 NM
questions.why: En route, GPS full-scale deflection is ±5 NM [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]]. Three-quarter scale is 0.75 x 5 = 3.75 NM. That is right at the ACS limit of three-quarter scale (ACS IR.V.B.S7), and you must fly the route centerline unless ATC says otherwise [[60:482|14 CFR 91.181]]. 0.75 NM would be terminal scale, and 0.23 NM approach scale.

questions.q: A STAR ends on the 12 DME arc of a VORTAC. Your DME has failed, but your WAAS GPS works. The VORTAC the arc is based on is not in your GPS database. A nearby airport waypoint is. What do you do?
options: Fly the arc by GPS distance from the nearby airport waypoint.
Make a user waypoint at the VORTAC's position and use it.
Fly the arc by keeping the VOR needle near the wingtip.
Tell ATC you can't fly the arc and ask for another routing.
questions.why: To fly a DME arc by GPS, the only acceptable active waypoint is the DME facility the arc is based on. If that facility is not in your database, you are not authorized to do it, and the positions must come from the database [[23:270|IFH 9-27]]. With the DME failed and GPS not authorized for this arc, report the malfunction to ATC and ask for another routing [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

questions.q: Departing a nontowered airport in IMC, you fly the textual ODP: "climb heading 330 to 4,000 before turning." Passing 2,500, Center says "Turn right heading 060, maintain 3,000." What is true?
options: Turn to 060, but keep climbing to 4,000 first, as the ODP requires.
Refuse the clearance. ATC can never change an altitude on an ODP.
The ODP is canceled. ATC now takes over terrain and obstacle clearance.
Keep heading 330 until 4,000, then turn right to heading 060.
questions.why: ATC may vector you off an ODP or give you an altitude lower than one on it. The ODP is then canceled, and ATC assumes responsibility for terrain and obstacle clearance [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h3]]. Paragraph h9 says ATC can't cancel or amend the crossing altitudes on an ODP [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9h9]], but h3 says a vector off the ODP, or an altitude lower than one on it, cancels the ODP itself. That is what happened here.

questions.q: You cross directly over a VORTAC. The DME reads 1.2 NM, but the GPS distance to the same VORTAC reads 0.0. What explains the difference?
options: The DME is out of tolerance and needs a check before any further IFR use.
The DME is locked on a different station by the HOLD function you left on.
GPS distance is slant range, so it reads lower than DME right over the station.
DME measures slant range, so overhead it shows your height above the station.
questions.why: DME measures the straight line from your antenna to the station, called slant range. The error is greatest close to the station, where the DME shows your altitude above the facility in NM. GPS distance is horizontal [[23:262|IFH 9-19]]. A HOLD function keeps the DME on an earlier station, but nothing here suggests that [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].

questions.q: Your IFR GPS is TSO-C129 (no WAAS). Before an IFR departure, the RAIM prediction shows an outage during the RNAV SID you planned. What should you do?
options: Fly the RNAV SID. The box will warn you if anything goes wrong.
Load the SID's waypoints by hand so the box won't need RAIM.
Fly the SID and watch the VOR only if a RAIM alert appears.
Ask for a non-RNAV departure, or delay until RAIM is available.
questions.why: When RAIM is predicted to be unavailable, rely on other approved navigation, reroute, delay or cancel [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. An RNAV departure must be loaded by name from the database, not built from waypoints [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16a2]]. If you can't meet an RNAV procedure's requirements, tell ATC "unable RNAV" [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16a1]].

questions.q: Arriving, you are cleared to fly a 12 DME arc to join the localizer. The chart shows a lead radial (LR) before the final course. You have one VOR/LOC receiver. What do you do at the LR?
options: Switch to the localizer and start a half-standard-rate turn.
Tune the localizer, but keep flying the arc until the needle centers.
Keep the VOR tuned until the arc crosses the localizer course.
Turn now and switch to the localizer once lined up with final.
questions.why: At the lead radial, a pilot with a single VOR/LOC receiver sets it to the localizer frequency. These lead radials give 7° of lead, so use a half-standard-rate turn until the LOC needle starts to move toward center [[23:262|IFH 9-19]]. As with a radial, start the intercepting turn when you reach the lead point [[23:261|IFH 9-18]]. Waiting for the needle to center means overshooting. When the arc meets the course at more than 90°, the LR gives at least 2 NM of lead [[29:183|IPH 4-43]].

questions.q: ATC says "Cross the 10 DME fix inbound at 4,000." You are at 8,000 ft, flying inbound at 120 knots groundspeed, and plan a 500 fpm descent. At what DME reading should you start down?
options: 34 DME
18 DME
16 DME
26 DME
questions.why: Plan the descent so you arrive at the crossing altitude [[29:120|IPH 3-8]]. You must lose 4,000 ft: 4,000 / 500 = 8 minutes. At 120 knots you cover 2 NM per minute, so 8 x 2 = 16 NM. Add that to the 10 DME fix: start down at 26 DME. That far out, slant range error is negligible [[23:262|IFH 9-19]].

questions.q: Your airway has an MEA of 5,000 ft. The intersection ahead is defined by a radial from an off-airway VOR and shows an MRA of 7,000 ft. You are cleared at 5,000. What does the MRA mean, and how can you still identify the fix?
options: It is a crossing altitude. Climb to 7,000 before you reach the fix, then level.
Below 7,000 you may not get the cross radial. An IFR GPS can find the fix.
Obstacles near the fix need 7,000. Climb now and descend after passing it.
7,000 is the highest altitude with good signals. Stay below it to keep reception.
questions.why: The MRA is the lowest altitude at which the intersection can be determined [[29:95|IPH 2-35]]. Reception is line of sight, so below it you may not get the cross radial from the off-airway VOR [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]. The VOR still works, so this is not the AIM's out-of-service case ("NAVAID information is not available"). Instead a suitable RNAV system may be used as an alternate means of navigation for an operating VOR, without monitoring the VOR [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3a2]], and it may find your position relative to a named fix defined by a VOR radial [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3c1]]. A climb-to-by-the-fix altitude is an MCA [[23:26|IFH 1-7]], and the highest usable altitude is the MAA [[29:95|IPH 2-35]].

questions.q: You fly a T-route in IMC. Your GPS shows a position error message and the map jumps 3 miles. You have a working VOR receiver, and Victor airways run nearby. What should you tell ATC?
options: Nothing yet. Wait to see whether the GPS recovers on its own.
Declare an emergency and ask for a block of altitudes to sort it out.
Report the GPS anomaly and its location, and say unable RNAV.
Ask for a higher altitude so the GPS can see more satellites.
questions.why: Report GPS anomalies to ATC without being asked, including location and altitude [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(h)]]. T-routes require GPS [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]], so say "unable RNAV, request amended clearance" [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16a1]]. Switch to another navigation source, such as the VOR [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]].

questions.q: You are flying an RNAV 1 SID with the GPS correctly at terminal sensitivity. The CDI shows half-scale deflection. How far off course are you, and is that within RNAV 1 accuracy?
options: About 2.5 NM, which is outside what RNAV 1 allows.
About 0.15 NM, since departures use approach scale.
About 0.5 NM, inside the 1 NM that RNAV 1 allows.
About 0.5 NM, which already breaks the 0.3 NM RNAV 1 limit.
questions.why: Published departures are flown with the GPS at terminal sensitivity, ±1 NM full scale [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]], so half scale is about 0.5 NM. RNAV 1 requires a total system error of no more than 1 NM for 95 percent of the flight time [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9i1]]. Still, correct back to the centerline. 2.5 NM assumes en route scale [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]].

questions.q: At the MEA in the mountains, Center stops answering your calls. Your VOR needle and ident are fine. What explains this, and what should you do first?
options: The MEA promises radio contact, so your radio failed. Squawk 7600 right away.
The MEA doesn't promise radio contact. Wait a minute, then try other frequencies.
The MEA only covers obstacles, so the VOR is also unreliable here and Center is out.
You are above the MAA. Descend to the MOCA to get radio contact back right away.
questions.why: MEA compliance does not necessarily guarantee communication [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]. Wait at least 1 minute before deciding the Center frequency failed. Then try the last controller, another Center frequency, or Flight Service [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1c]].

questions.q: Center offers "Proceed direct Alpha VOR, descend at pilot's discretion, maintain 4,000." The direct path is off airways over hills. If you accept, what changes for you?
options: Nothing. ATC is now responsible for all of your terrain clearance on this route.
You share terrain clearance, so know the highest terrain on the route.
You must hold your altitude until you are back on an airway or the route ends.
You may descend, then climb back up to an earlier altitude if you meet icing.
questions.why: Pilots who accept an off-airway direct clearance also accept shared responsibility for terrain clearance, so know the highest terrain and obstacles around you [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]. With a pilot's discretion descent you may level off, but once you leave an altitude you may not return to it [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].

questions.q: Level at 9,000 ft, you hear "Descend and maintain 5,000." How should you fly the descent?
options: Start promptly at an optimum rate to 6,000, then 500 to 1,500 fpm to 5,000.
Start down when you like, and level off on the way if you want, at any rate.
Descend at exactly 500 fpm all the way down to 5,000, starting at once.
Start down within 5 minutes at a comfortable rate, then report reaching 5,000.
questions.why: "Descend and maintain" calls for a prompt response: descend at the optimum rate until 1,000 ft above the assigned altitude, then at 500 to 1,500 fpm [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]. Starting when you like and leveling off on the way is a pilot's discretion descent. Report leaving 9,000 for the new altitude [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(a)]].
